source.title: Chaotic Regularization and Heavy-Tailed Limits for Deterministic Gradient Descent
source.authors: S. H. Lim; Yijun Wan; Umut Simsekli

record.tranche_reason: The study trains with deterministic chaotic perturbations and reports held-out performance and train-test gaps, using a different intervention from the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own outcomes for MPGD, Gaussian perturbations, and vanilla GD on Airfoil, CIFAR-10, and ECG. These results bear on generalization but do not test a listed version directly. Cited results from prior work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether chaotic perturbations improve gradient descent, which is outside V1–V8. Its Hessian analysis does not test magnitude-aware sharpness as a predictor of generalization gaps. The mini-batch SGD accuracy is cited from another study and uses a different training recipe and epoch budget, so it does not test V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors: MPGD provides a theoretical framework for chaotic perturbed GD, with a heavy-tailed SDE limit, a conditional generalization bound, and implicit regularization analysis, alongside empirical advantages. They explicitly do not claim a competitive algorithm outperforming SGD. Empirical improvement depends on parameters and is not uniform across all reported measures.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces deterministic chaotic perturbations to gradient descent (MPGD), then compares with vanilla GD and Gaussian perturbations; it does not reproduce the original study methods named in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Airfoil outcomes vary with γ and β; authors say larger γ does not guarantee better test performance and parameters require tuning. On CIFAR-10, MPGD consistently outperforms vanilla GD for smaller step-sizes, while both perform similarly at a large step-size. ECG results depend on γ and β; larger perturbation levels can cause instability and fluctuations.

fits_no_version.finding: On Airfoil, MPGD reduces test RMSE at gamma 0.55–0.65, but increases it at 0.7 relative to vanilla GD. Its RMSE gaps are below vanilla GD across these settings, though not consistently below Gaussian perturbations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Chaotic perturbations can improve regression generalization, with outcomes depending on perturbation parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Full-batch ResNet-18 with MPGD achieves 73.72–75.97% validation accuracy versus 73.10% for vanilla GD, with smaller accuracy gaps; Gaussian perturbations achieve 70.58%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Chaotic perturbations can improve full-batch GD performance under the tested fixed-learning-rate CIFAR-10 recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: On ECG, MPGD achieves 88.22–94.87% mean test accuracy versus 58.38% for vanilla GD and 65.68% for Gaussian perturbations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Chaotic perturbations can improve held-out accuracy when baseline gradient descent makes little optimization progress.

fits_no_version.finding: The weak-perturbation analysis introduces a covariance-weighted Hessian term, and the synthetic widening-valley experiment shows reduced Hessian trace. Neither measures magnitude-aware sharpness or its correlation with held-out gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Chaotic perturbations can favor flatter regions of a synthetic optimization landscape.

record.problems: The generalization bound is for the limiting SDE and depends on implicit constants and mutual-information terms for which the authors say they cannot provide quantitative estimates. The CIFAR-10 experiment uses fixed, untuned step-size; the authors report lower accuracies than the reference mini-batch SGD and acknowledge that additional tuning and tricks could improve results. The experiments average 5 seeds; standard deviations are reported in appendices.
record.rows_left_out: For Airfoil, the table also reports parenthesized results for variant (11), omitted to keep the catalog focused on the main MPGD recursion (8). Appendix Tables 4–6 report standard deviations and additional β settings, not extracted as separate rows. Appendix Table 3 parenthesized variant (11) results are omitted. These supplementary tables report variability or alternate variants rather than additional versions of the claim.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance compared with natural-label training under the same recipe.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets and recovery interventions.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and joint dropout/weight-decay removal.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with gaps among similarly fitted networks, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All recorded means match the supplied tables. These are valid results for the study's own method but provide no verdict on V1–V8. Uncertainty is reported in Tables 3, 4, and 6 despite each row saying otherwise. The GitHub URL identifies the implementation adapted for CIFAR-10, rather than establishing release of the authors' MPGD code.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label test accuracy.
No width sweep or test-error comparison beyond the width needed to fit training data.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD or momentum SGD.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
The paper discusses Hessian reduction and flatter minima, but does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or test whether it ranks train-test gaps.
No removal of memorized examples or retraining comparison.
